'''Eugene Earle van Tamelen''' (July 20, 1925 &ndash; December 12, 2009) was an [[organic chemistry|organic chemist]] who is  especially recognized for his contributions to bioorganic chemistry.<ref name=NYTObit>{{cite news|title=Eugene van Tamelen, 84, Dies; Chemist Inspired by Nature|first=Kenneth|last=Chang|date=December 29, 2009|access-date=December 31, 2009|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/12/30/science/30tamelen.html}}</ref>

van Tamelen published five papers while an undergraduate at [[Hope College]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Van Tamelen | first1 = Eugene E. | last2 = Van Zyl | first2 = Gerrit | year = 1949 | title = Malonic ester reaction with 1-halo nitro paraffins | journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume = 71 | issue = 3| pages = 835–7 | doi = 10.1021/ja01171a020 }}</ref> He conducted graduate work at [[Harvard University]], receiving his doctorate in 1950 with [[Gilbert Stork]] as his advisor. He began his academic career at the [[University of Wisconsin]], later joining the faculty of [[Stanford University]], where he spent the majority of his career. Among his many students was Nobelist [[K. Barry Sharpless]].

He led a team who were the first persons to achieve the total synthesis of [[yohimbine]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=van Tamelen|first1=E.E.|last2=Shamma|first2=Maurice|last3=Burgstahler|first3=Albert|last4=Tamm|first4=Rudolph|last5=Aldrich|first5=Paul|journal=[[J. Am. Chem. Soc.]] |title=The Total Synthesis of Yohimbine |year=1958 |volume=80|issue=18|pages=5006–5007 |doi=10.1021/ja01551a062}}</ref>  He pioneered in what is today called [[biomimetic synthesis]]. He was the first to identify [[squalene oxide]] as a precursor in the [[biosynthesis]] of [[cholesterol]].<ref>E. E. van Tamelen "The Role of Organic Synthesis in Bioorganic Chemistry" Pure Appl. Chem., 1981, Vol. 53, No. 6, pp. 1259-1270.  {{doi|10.1351/pac198153061259}}.</ref> Van Tamelen was also the first to synthesise [[Dewar benzene]].  He developed a system for [[nitrogen fixation]] using [[titanocene]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Van Tamelen | first1 = Eugene E | year = 1970 | title = Design and development of an organic-inorganic system for the chemical modification of molecular nitrogen under mild conditions | journal = Accounts of Chemical Research | volume = 3 | issue = 11| pages = 361–7 | doi = 10.1021/ar50035a001 }}</ref>

van Tamelen was also the owner of the first [[Marshall Erdman]]-built [[Frank Lloyd Wright]]-designed pre-fabricated house, commonly known as the "Eugene van Tamelen House".<ref name=UNL>{{citation|title=Eugene Van Tamelen House (Erdman Prefab I)|access-date=April 18, 2012|url=http://contentdm.unl.edu/cdm4/item_viewer.php?CISOROOT=/archivision&CISOPTR=34105&CISOBOX=1&REC=16|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121212122724/http://contentdm.unl.edu/cdm4/item_viewer.php?CISOROOT=/archivision&CISOPTR=34105&CISOBOX=1&REC=16|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 12, 2012}}</ref>

In 1981, van Tamelen became a founding member of the [[World Cultural Council]].<ref>{{cite web | title = About Us | publisher = [[World Cultural Council]] | url = https://www.consejoculturalmundial.org/about-us/ | access-date = November 8, 2016}}</ref>

Eugene van Tamelen died of cancer in 2009.

==Awards==
Among his awards, he received the [[ACS Award in Pure Chemistry]] in 1961 and was elected to the US [[National Academy of Sciences]].
